Spent the last two Saturdays helping a buddy redo the electric in his shed, and I’m putting this here because it was funny right up until you think about what could’ve happened.

The shed had “power” when we started. What it actually had was three orange extension cords daisy-chained out a basement window, across the yard, and under the deck. Nothing says permanent wiring like moving the electric before you mow.

Then I opened things up and found:

- One splice wrapped in duct tape. Not electrical tape. Duct tape. Very handy if the circuit also needed a suitcase repaired.
- A 30-amp breaker feeding 14-gauge wire. For anybody who doesn’t do this: that wire belongs on a 15-amp breaker. Putting it on a 30 doesn’t give it “more room.” It lets the wire get in trouble long before the breaker does its job.
- An outlet hooked up with speaker wire. Apparently if it can make the Steelers game louder, it can run a refrigerator.
- A “GFCI” that was just a regular outlet with a GFCI sticker stuck on it. I have a Steelers sticker on my truck. That does not make my truck a Steeler.
- A ceiling fan box held up with one drywall screw. One. I’ve hung wall calendars with more support.
- A mouse nest inside a junction box. Mice were fine. Unbothered. Little guys looked at me like I was there about their permit.

Best part: inside the panel door, written in Sharpie, was:

SHED - DONT TOUCH - RON

The wife was standing there when I opened it and goes, “Who’s Ron?” Like I’m supposed to know. Lady, I just got here. I don’t know Ron. I do know he didn’t want anybody touching it, which was the first thing all day I agreed with him on.

I trenched 18 inches, ran 12/2 UF, put in a 20-amp GFCI breaker, installed real boxes and real outlets, and mounted the fan on an actual brace. Now the fan turns, the outlets work, and nothing smells like it’s preheating.

I’m not posting this to say the previous guy was some evil mastermind. He probably wasn’t evil at all. He was cheap and a little proud of himself, and that describes a whole lot of the messes electricians get called in to fix.

“It worked fine” is not the same thing as “it was safe.” Sometimes the only difference between “it worked fine for years” and a fire is that the right combination of bad things hasn’t happened yet. A dried-out extension cord, a overloaded outlet, a loose connection, one mouse deciding the speaker wire looks delicious — now everybody’s standing in the driveway wondering how it happened.

And I get it. Everybody wants to save money, and everybody knows a guy. But if the guy’s entire qualification is that he watched a bunch of YouTube videos and owns a Klein screwdriver, call a licensed electrician. Not your buddy with a video and “a pretty good idea how it works.”

Ask questions. Get the right wire, the right breaker, real connections, real boxes, and the protection that’s supposed to be there. A shed, garage, freezer outlet, ceiling fan — none of it is worth burning your house down over.

Total bill for this one: two pizzas and a case of Yuengling. So yes, sometimes you can still get a deal. Just don’t let Ron pay you in extension cords.
